title: Repairs
heading: Repairing Partitions#
text: If you have experienced a loss of object replicas in your cluster, you may need to perform a repair operation on one or more of your data partitions. Repairs of Riak KV data are typically run in situations where partitions or whole nodes are lost due to corruption or hardware failure. In these cases, nodes or partitions are brought back online without any data, which means that the need to repair data will depend mainly on your use case and on whether active anti-entropy is enabled.

title: Repairs
heading: Repairing Partitions#
text: Repairs of Riak KV data are typically run in situations where partitions or whole nodes are lost due to corruption or hardware failure. In these cases, nodes or partitions are brought back online without any data, which means that the need to repair data will depend mainly on your use case and on whether active anti-entropy is enabled. You will need to run a repair if the following are both true:

title: Repairs
heading: Repairing Partitions#
text: You will need to run a repair if the following are both true: Active anti-entropy is disabled You have both non-expiring data and keys that are not accessed frequently (which means that they are not likely to be subject to read repair)

title: Repairs
heading: Repairing Partitions#
text: You will most likely not need to run a repair operation if any of the following is true:

title: Repairs
heading: Repairing Partitions#
text: You will most likely not need to run a repair operation if any of the following is true: Active anti-entropy is enabled Your entire key set is accessed frequently, allowing passive read repair to repair the partitions Your data expires frequently

title: Repairs
heading: Repairing Partitions#
text: In most cases, we recommend either using active anti-entropy or, if necessary and only when necessary, running a repair operation using the instructions below.

title: Repairs
heading: Running a Repair#
text: The Riak KV repair operation will repair objects from a node’s adjacent partitions on the ring, consequently fixing the index. This is done as efficiently as possible by generating a hash range for all the buckets and thus avoiding a preflist calculation for each key. Only a hash of each key is done, its range determined from a bucket->range map, and then the hash is checked against the range.

title: Repairs
heading: Running a Repair#
text: This is done as efficiently as possible by generating a hash range for all the buckets and thus avoiding a preflist calculation for each key. Only a hash of each key is done, its range determined from a bucket->range map, and then the hash is checked against the range. Repairs are not allowed to occur during ownership changes.

title: Repairs
heading: Running a Repair#
text: Only a hash of each key is done, its range determined from a bucket->range map, and then the hash is checked against the range. Repairs are not allowed to occur during ownership changes. Since ownership entails the moving of partition data it is safest to make them mutually exclusive events.

title: Repairs
heading: Running a Repair#
text: Repairs are not allowed to occur during ownership changes. Since ownership entails the moving of partition data it is safest to make them mutually exclusive events. If you join or remove a node all repairs across the entire cluster will be killed.

title: Repairs
heading: Repairing a Single Partition#
text: In the case of data loss in a single partition, only that partition can be repaired.

title: Repairs
heading: Repairing a Single Partition#
text: In the case of data loss in a single partition, only that partition can be repaired. From any node in the cluster, attach to Riak’s Erlang shell: Bash riak attach You may have to hit Enter again to get a console prompt. Execute the repair for a single partition using the below command: Erlang riak_kv_vnode:repair(»Partition ID«). where `»Partition_ID«` is replaced by the ID of the partition to repair. For example: Erlang riak_kv_vnode:repair(251195593916248939066258330623111144003363405824). Once the command has been executed, detach from Riak using `Control-C`.

title: Repairs
heading: Repairing All Partitions on a Node#
text: If a node is lost, all partitions currently owned by that node can be repaired.

title: Repairs
heading: Repairing All Partitions on a Node#
text: If a node is lost, all partitions currently owned by that node can be repaired. From any node in the cluster, attach to Riak’s Erlang shell: Bash riak attach Get a copy of the current Ring: Erlang {ok, Ring} = riak_core_ring_manager:get_my_ring(). You will get a lot of output with ring record information. You can safely ignore it.

title: Repairs
heading: Repairing All Partitions on a Node#
text: Get a list of partitions owned by the node that needs to be repaired. Replace `dev1@127.0.0.1` with the name of the node to be repaired. The name can be found in each node’s `vm.args` file, specified as the `-name` parameter, if you are using the older configuration system; if you are using the newer, `riak-conf`-based system, the name is given by the `nodename` parameter. Erlang Partitions = [P || {P, 'dev1@127.0.0.1'} <- riak_core_ring:all_owners(Ring)]. Note: The above is an Erlang list comprehension that loops over each `{Partition, Node}` tuple in the ring and extracts only the partitions that match the given node name, as a list.

title: Repairs
heading: Repairing All Partitions on a Node#
text: Execute the repair on all the partitions. Executing the repairs all at once will cause a lot of `{shutdown, max_concurrency}` messages in the logs. These can be safely ingored, as it is just the transfers mechanism enforcing an upper limit on the number of concurrent transfers. Erlang [riak_kv_vnode:repair(P) || P <- Partitions]. Once the command has been executed, detach from Riak using `Control-C`.

title: Repairs
heading: Monitoring Repairs#
text: The above repair commands can be monitored via the `riak admin transfers` command.

title: Repairs
heading: Killing a Repair#
text: Currently there is no easy way to kill an individual repair. The only option is to kill all repairs targeting a given node. This is done by running `riak_core_vnode_manager:kill_repairs(Reason)` on the node undergoing repair.

title: Repairs
heading: Killing a Repair#

title: Repairs

heading: Killing a Repair#
text: Erlang riak_core_vnode_manager:kill_repairs(killed_by_user).

title: Repairs
heading: Killing a Repair#
text: Log entries will reflect that repairs were killed manually, and will look similar to: Text

title: Repairs
heading: Killing a Repair#
text: Text 2012-08-10 10:14:50.529 [warning] <0.154.0>@riak_core_vnode_manager:handle_cast:395 Killing all repairs: killed_by_user

title: Repairs

text: Repairs on a node can also be killed remotely from another node in the cluster. From a `riak attach` session the below command can be used: Erlang

title: Repairs
heading: Killing a Repair#
text: Erlang rpc:call('dev1@127.0.0.1', riak_core_vnode_manager, kill_repairs, [killed_by_user]).

When you’re done, press `Ctrl-D` to disconnect the console. DO NOT RUN q() which will cause the running Riak node to quit. Note that `Ctrl-D` merely disconnects the console from the service, it does not stop the code from running.

title: Security Basics
text: Note on Network security This document covers only the 2.0 authentication and authorization features. For a look at network security in Riak, see Security and Firewalls.

title: Security Basics
text: This document covers only the 2.0 authentication and authorization features. For a look at network security in Riak, see Security and Firewalls. As of version 2.0, Riak administrators can selectively apportion access to a wide variety of Riak’s functionality, including accessing, modifying, and deleting objects, changing bucket properties, and running MapReduce jobs.

title: Security Basics
heading: Terminology#
text: Authentication is the process of identifying a user. Authorization is verifying whether a user has access to perform the requested operation. Groups can have permissions assigned to them, but cannot be authenticated. Users can be authenticated and authorized; permissions (authorization) may be granted directly or via group membership. Sources are used to define authentication mechanisms. A user cannot be authenticated to Riak until a source is defined.

title: Security Basics
heading: Security Checklist#
text: There are a few key steps that all applications will need to undertake when turning on Riak security. Missing one of these steps will almost certainly break your application, so make sure that you have done each of the following before enabling security:

title: Security Basics
heading: Security Checklist#
text: Missing one of these steps will almost certainly break your application, so make sure that you have done each of the following before enabling security: Because Riak security requires a secure SSL connection, you will need to generate appropriate SSL certs, enable SSL and establish a certificate configuration on each node. If you enable security without having established a functioning SSL connection, all requests to Riak will fail. Define users and, optionally, groups Define an authentication source for each user Grant the necessary permissions to each user (and/or group) Check any Erlang MapReduce code for invocations of Riak modules other than `riak_kv_mapreduce`. Enabling security will prevent those from succeeding unless those modules are available via the `add_path` mechanism documented in Installing Custom Code. Make sure that your client software will work properly: It must pass authentication information with each request It must support HTTPS or encrypted Protocol Buffers traffic If using HTTPS, the proper port (presumably 443) is open from client to server Code that uses Riak’s deprecated link walking feature will not work with security enabled It must pass authentication information with each request

title: Security Basics
heading: Security Checklist#
text: It must support HTTPS or encrypted Protocol Buffers traffic If using HTTPS, the proper port (presumably 443) is open from client to server Code that uses Riak’s deprecated link walking feature will not work with security enabled If you have applications that rely on an already existing Riak cluster, make sure that those applications are prepared to gracefully transition into using Riak security once security is enabled.

title: Security Basics
heading: Security Checklist#
text: Security should be enabled only after all of the above steps have been performed and your security setup has been properly vetted. Clients that use Protocol Buffers will typically have to be reconfigured/restarted with the proper credentials once security is enabled.

title: Security Basics
heading: Security Basics#
text: Riak security may be checked, enabled, or disabled by an administrator through the command line. This allows an administrator to change security settings for the whole cluster quickly without needing to change settings on a node-by-node basis. Note: Currently, Riak security commands can be run only through the command line, using the `riak admin security` command.

title: Security Basics
heading: Security Basics#
text: This allows an administrator to change security settings for the whole cluster quickly without needing to change settings on a node-by-node basis. Note: Currently, Riak security commands can be run only through the command line, using the `riak admin security` command. In future versions of Riak, administrators may have the option of issuing those commands through the Protocol Buffers and HTTP interfaces.

title: Security Basics
heading: Enabling Security#
text: Warning: Enable security with caution Enabling security will change the way your client libraries and your applications interact with Riak. Once security is enabled, all client connections must be encrypted and all permissions will be denied by default.

title: Security Basics
heading: Enabling Security#
text: Enabling security will change the way your client libraries and your applications interact with Riak. Once security is enabled, all client connections must be encrypted and all permissions will be denied by default. Do not enable this in production until you have worked through the security checklist above and tested everything in a non-production environment.

title: Security Basics
heading: Enabling Security#
text: Once security is enabled, all client connections must be encrypted and all permissions will be denied by default. Do not enable this in production until you have worked through the security checklist above and tested everything in a non-production environment. Riak security is disabled by default.

title: Security Basics
heading: Enabling Security#

title: Security Basics

title: Security Basics
heading: Enabling Security#
text: Bash riak admin security enable

title: Security Basics
heading: Enabling Security#
text: As per the warning above, do not enable security in production without taking the appropriate precautions. All users, groups, authentication sources, and permissions can be configured while security is disabled, allowing you to create a security configuration of any level of complexity without prematurely impacting the service. This should be borne in mind when you are managing users and managing sources.

title: Security Basics
heading: Disabling Security#
text: If you disable security, this means that you have disabled all of the various permissions checks that take place when executing operations against Riak. Users, groups, and other security attributes remain available for configuration while security is disabled, and will be applied if and when security is re-enabled. Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Disabling Security#
text: Bash riak admin security disable

title: Security Basics
heading: Disabling Security#
text: While security is disabled, clients will need to be reconfigured to no longer require TLS and send credentials.

title: Security Basics

title: Security Basics
heading: Checking Security Status#
text: This command will usually return `Enabled` or `Disabled`, but if security is enabled on a mixed-mode cluster (running a combination of Riak 2.0 and older versions) it will indicate that security is enabled but not yet available.

title: Security Basics
heading: User Management#
text: Riak security enables you to control authorization by creating, modifying, and deleting user characteristics and granting users selective access to Riak functionality (and also to revoke access). Users can be assigned one or more of the following characteristics:

title: Security Basics
heading: User Management#
text: Users can be assigned one or more of the following characteristics: `username` `groups` `password`

title: Security Basics
heading: User Management#
text: You may also assign users characteristics beyond those listed above—e.g., listing email addresses or other information—but those values will carry no special significance for Riak. Note: The `username` is the one user characteristic that cannot be changed once a user has been created.

The output will look like this if the user `riakuser` has been explicitly granted a `riak_kv.get` permission on the bucket `shopping_list` and inherits a set of permissions from the `admin` group: Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Add Group#
text: For easier management of permissions across several users, it is possible to create groups to be assigned to those users. Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Add Group#
text: Bash riak admin security add-group admin

title: Security Basics
heading: Add User#
text: To create a user with the username `riakuser`, we use the `add-user` command: Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Add User#
text: Bash riak admin security add-user riakuser

title: Security Basics
heading: Add User#
text: Using the command this way will create the user `riakuser` without any characteristics beyond a username, which is the only attribute that you must assign upon user creation. Alternatively, a password—or other attributes—can be assigned to the user upon creation. Here, we’ll assign a password:

title: Security Basics
heading: Add User#
text: Alternatively, a password—or other attributes—can be assigned to the user upon creation. Here, we’ll assign a password: Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Add User#
text: Bash riak admin security add-user riakuser password=Test1234

title: Security Basics
heading: Assigning a Password and Altering Existing User Characteristics#
text: While passwords and other characteristics can be set upon user creation, it often makes sense to change user characteristics after the user has already been created. Let’s say that the user `riakuser` was created without a password (or created with a password that we’d like to change). The `alter-user` command can be used to modify our `riakuser` user:

title: Security Basics
heading: Assigning a Password and Altering Existing User Characteristics#
text: Let’s say that the user `riakuser` was created without a password (or created with a password that we’d like to change). The `alter-user` command can be used to modify our `riakuser` user: Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Assigning a Password and Altering Existing User Characteristics#
text: Bash riak admin security alter-user riakuser password=opensesame

title: Security Basics
heading: Assigning a Password and Altering Existing User Characteristics#
text: When creating or altering a user, any number of `<option>=<value>` pairs can be appended to the end of the command. Any non-standard options will be stored and displayed via the `riak admin security print-users` command. Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Assigning a Password and Altering Existing User Characteristics#
text: Bash riak admin security alter-user riakuser name=bill age=47 fav_color=red

title: Security Basics
heading: Assigning a Password and Altering Existing User Characteristics#
text: Now, the `print-users` command should return this: Text

title: Security Basics
heading: Assigning a Password and Altering Existing User Characteristics#
text: Note: Usernames cannot be changed using the `alter-user` command. For example, running `riak admin security alter-user riakuser username=other-name`, will instead add the `{"username","other-name"}` tuple to `riakuser`’s options.

title: Security Basics
heading: Managing Groups for a User#
text: If we have a user `riakuser` and we’d like to assign her to the `admin` group, we assign the value `admin` to the option `groups`: Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Managing Groups for a User#
text: Bash riak admin security alter-user riakuser groups=admin

title: Security Basics
heading: Managing Groups for a User#
text: If we’d like to make the user `riakuser` both an `admin` and an `archoverlord`: Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Managing Groups for a User#
text: Bash riak admin security alter-user riakuser groups=admin,archoverlord

title: Security Basics
heading: Managing Groups for a User#
text: There is no way to incrementally add groups; even if `riakuser` was already an `admin`, it is necessary to list it again when adding the `archoverlord` group. Thus, to remove a group from a user, use `alter-user` and list all other groups. If the user should be removed from all groups, use `groups=` with no list:

title: Security Basics
heading: Managing Groups for a User#
text: Thus, to remove a group from a user, use `alter-user` and list all other groups. If the user should be removed from all groups, use `groups=` with no list: Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Managing Groups for a User#
text: Bash riak admin security alter-user riakuser groups=

title: Security Basics
heading: Managing Groups for Groups#
text: Groups can be added to other groups for cascading permissions. Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Managing Groups for Groups#
text: Bash riak admin security alter-group admin groups=dev

title: Security Basics
heading: Deleting a User or Group#
text: If you’d like to remove a user, use the `del-user` command: Text

title: Security Basics
heading: Deleting a User or Group#
text: Text riak admin security del-user riakuser

title: Security Basics
heading: Deleting a User or Group#
text: For groups, use the `del-group` command: Text

title: Security Basics
heading: Deleting a User or Group#
text: Text riak admin security del-group admin

title: Security Basics
heading: Adding or Deleting Multiple Users#
text: The `riak admin security` command does not currently allow you to add or delete multiple users using a single command. Instead, they must be added or deleted one by one.

title: Security Basics
heading: Managing Permissions#
text: Permission to perform a wide variety of operations against Riak can be granted to—or revoked from—users via the `grant` and `revoke` commands.

title: Security Basics
heading: Basic Form#
text: The `grant` command takes one of the following forms: Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Basic Form#
text: Bash riak admin security grant <permissions> on any to all|{<user>|<group>[,...]} riak admin security grant <permissions> on <bucket-type> to all|{<user>|<group>[,...]} riak admin security grant <permissions> on <bucket-type> <bucket> to all|{<user>|<group>[,...]}

title: Security Basics
heading: Basic Form#
text: The `revoke` command is essentially the same, except that `to` is replaced with `from` of `to`: Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Basic Form#
text: Bash riak admin security revoke <permissions> on any from all|{<user>|<group>[,...]} riak admin security revoke <permissions> on <bucket-type> from all|{<user>|<group>[,...]} riak admin security revoke <permissions> on <bucket-type> <bucket> from all|{<user>|<group>[,...]}

title: Security Basics
heading: Basic Form#
text: If you select `any`, this means that the permission (or set of permissions) is granted/revoked for all buckets and bucket types. If you specify a bucket type only, then the permission is granted/revoked for all buckets of that type. If you specify a bucket type and a bucket, the permission is granted/revoked only for that bucket type/bucket combination.

title: Security Basics
heading: Basic Form#
text: If you specify a bucket type only, then the permission is granted/revoked for all buckets of that type. If you specify a bucket type and a bucket, the permission is granted/revoked only for that bucket type/bucket combination. Note: You cannot grant/revoke permissions with respect to a bucket alone.

title: Security Basics
heading: Basic Form#
text: If you specify a bucket type and a bucket, the permission is granted/revoked only for that bucket type/bucket combination. Note: You cannot grant/revoke permissions with respect to a bucket alone. You must specify either a bucket type by itself or a bucket type and bucket.

heading: Basic Form#
text: Note: You cannot grant/revoke permissions with respect to a bucket alone. You must specify either a bucket type by itself or a bucket type and bucket. This limitation reflects the naming structure underlying buckets and bucket types.

title: Security Basics

When specifying the user(s)/group(s) to which you want to apply a permission (or set of permissions), you may list any number of users or groups comma-separated with no whitespace.

title: Security Basics

text: Selecting `all` grants or revokes a permission (or set of permissions) for all users in all groups. When specifying the user(s)/group(s) to which you want to apply a permission (or set of permissions), you may list any number of users or groups comma-separated with no whitespace. Here is an example of granting multiple permissions across all buckets and bucket types to multiple users:

title: Security Basics
heading: Basic Form#
text: When specifying the user(s)/group(s) to which you want to apply a permission (or set of permissions), you may list any number of users or groups comma-separated with no whitespace. Here is an example of granting multiple permissions across all buckets and bucket types to multiple users: Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Basic Form#
text: Bash riak admin security grant riak_kv.get,riak_search.query on any to jane,ahmed

title: Security Basics
heading: Basic Form#
text: If the same name is used for both a user and a group, the `grant` command will ask for the name to be prefixed with `user/` or `group/` to disambiguate.

title: Security Basics
heading: Key/Value Permissions#
text: Permissions that can be granted for basic key/value access functionality:

title: Security Basics
heading: Key/Value Permissions#
text: Permissions that can be granted for basic key/value access functionality: Permission Operation `riak_kv.get` Retrieve objects `riak_kv.put` Create or update objects `riak_kv.delete` Delete objects `riak_kv.index` Index objects using secondary indexes (2i) `riak_kv.list_keys` List all of the keys in a bucket `riak_kv.list_buckets` List all buckets

title: Security Basics
heading: Key/Value Permissions#
text: Note on Listing Keys and Buckets `riak_kv.list_keys` and `riak_kv.list_buckets` are both very expensive operations that should be performed very rarely and never in production. Access to this functionality should be granted very carefully. If you’d like to create, for example, a `client` account that is allowed only to run `GET` and `PUT` requests on all buckets:

title: Security Basics
heading: Key/Value Permissions#
text: Access to this functionality should be granted very carefully. If you’d like to create, for example, a `client` account that is allowed only to run `GET` and `PUT` requests on all buckets: Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Key/Value Permissions#
text: Bash riak admin security add-user client riak admin security grant riak_kv.get,riak_kv.put on any to client

title: Security Basics
heading: MapReduce Permissions#
text: Permission to perform MapReduce jobs can be assigned using `riak_kv.mapreduce`. The following example grants MapReduce permissions to the user `mapreduce-power-user` for all buckets and bucket types: Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: MapReduce Permissions#
text: Bash riak admin security grant riak_kv.mapreduce on any to mapreduce-power-user

title: Security Basics
heading: Bucket Type Permissions#
text: In versions 2.0 and later, Riak users can manage bucket types in addition to setting bucket properties. `riak admin security` allows you to manage the following bucket type-related permissions:

title: Security Basics
heading: Bucket Type Permissions#
text: In versions 2.0 and later, Riak users can manage bucket types in addition to setting bucket properties. `riak admin security` allows you to manage the following bucket type-related permissions: Permission Operation `riak_core.get_bucket` Retrieve the `props` associated with a bucket `riak_core.set_bucket` Modify the `props` associated with a bucket `riak_core.get_bucket_type` Retrieve the set of `props` associated with a bucket type `riak_core.set_bucket_type` Modify the set of `props` associated with a bucket type

title: Security Basics
heading: Managing Sources#
text: While user management enables you to control authorization with regard to users, security sources provide you with an interface for managing means of authentication. If you create users and grant them access to some or all of Riak’s functionality as described in the User Management section, you will then need to define security sources required for authentication. An more in-depth tutorial can be found in Managing Security Sources.

title: Security Basics
heading: Add Source#
text: Riak security sources may be applied to a specific user, multiple users, or all users (`all`).

title: Security Basics
heading: Available Sources#
text: Source Description `trust` Always authenticates successfully if access has been granted to a user or all users on the specified CIDR range `password` Check the user’s password against the PBKFD2-hashed password stored in Riak `pam` Authenticate against the given pluggable authentication module (PAM) service `certificate` Authenticate using a client certificate

title: Security Basics
heading: Example: Adding a Trusted Source#
text: Security sources can be added either to a specific user, multiple users, or all users (`all`). In general, the `add-source` command takes the following form: Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Example: Adding a Trusted Source#
text: Bash riak admin security add-source all|<users> <CIDR> <source> [<option>=<value>[...]]

title: Security Basics
heading: Example: Adding a Trusted Source#
text: Using `all` indicates that the authentication source can be added to all users. A source can be added to a specific user, e.g. `add-source superuser`, or to a list of users separated by commas, e.g. `add-source jane,bill,admin`. Let’s say that we want to give all users trusted access to securables (without a password) when requests come from `localhost`:

title: Security Basics
heading: Example: Adding a Trusted Source#
text: A source can be added to a specific user, e.g. `add-source superuser`, or to a list of users separated by commas, e.g. `add-source jane,bill,admin`. Let’s say that we want to give all users trusted access to securables (without a password) when requests come from `localhost`: Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Example: Adding a Trusted Source#
text: Bash riak admin security add-source all 127.0.0.1/32 trust

title: Security Basics
heading: Example: Adding a Trusted Source#
text: At that point, the `riak admin security print-sources` command would print the following: Text

title: Security Basics
heading: Deleting Sources#
text: If we wish to remove the `trust` source that we granted to `all` in the example above, we can simply use the `del-source` command and specify the CIDR. Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Deleting Sources#
text: Bash riak admin security del-source all 127.0.0.1/32

title: Security Basics
heading: Deleting Sources#
text: Note that this does not require that you specify which type of source is being deleted. You only need to specify the user(s) or `all`, because only one source can be applied to a user or `all` at any given time. The following command would remove the source for `riakuser` on `localhost`, regardless of which source is being used:

title: Security Basics
heading: Deleting Sources#
text: You only need to specify the user(s) or `all`, because only one source can be applied to a user or `all` at any given time. The following command would remove the source for `riakuser` on `localhost`, regardless of which source is being used: Bash

title: Security Basics
heading: Deleting Sources#
text: Bash riak admin security del-source riakuser 127.0.0.1/32

title: Security Basics
heading: Deleting Sources#
text: Note on Removing Sources If you apply a security source both to `all` and to specific users and then wish to remove that source, you will need to do so in separate steps. The `riak admin security del-source all ...` command by itself is not sufficient. For example, if you have assigned the source `password` to both `all` and to the user `riakuser` on the network `127.0.0.1/32`, the following two-step process would be required to fully remove the source: Bash riak admin security del-source all 127.0.0.1/32 password riak admin security del-source riakuser 127.0.0.1/32 password

title: Security Basics
heading: More Usage Examples#
text: This section provides only a very brief overview of the syntax for working with sources. For more information on using the `trust`, `password`, `pam`, and `certificate` sources, please see our Managing Security Sources document.

title: Security Basics
heading: Enabling SSL#
text: In order to use any authentication or authorization features, you must enable SSL for Riak. SSL is disabled by default, but you will need to enable it prior to enabling security. If you are using Protocol Buffers as a transport protocol for Riak (which we strongly recommend), enabling SSL on a given node requires only that you specify a host and port for the node as well as a certification configuration.

title: Security Basics
heading: Enabling SSL#
text: SSL is disabled by default, but you will need to enable it prior to enabling security. If you are using Protocol Buffers as a transport protocol for Riak (which we strongly recommend), enabling SSL on a given node requires only that you specify a host and port for the node as well as a certification configuration. If, however, you are using the HTTP API for Riak and would like to configure HTTPS, you will need to not only establish a certificate configuration but also specify an HTTPS host and port.

heading: TLS Settings#
text: Three things to note:

title: Security Basics
heading: Certificate Configuration#
text: If you are using any of the available security sources, including trust-based authentication, you will need to do so over a secure SSL connection. In order to establish a secure connection, you will need to ensure that each Riak node’s configuration files point to the proper paths for your generated certs. By default, Riak assumes that all certs are stored in each node’s `/etc` directory.

title: Security Basics
heading: Certificate Configuration#
text: In order to establish a secure connection, you will need to ensure that each Riak node’s configuration files point to the proper paths for your generated certs. By default, Riak assumes that all certs are stored in each node’s `/etc` directory. If you are using the newer, `riak.conf`-based configuration system, you can change the location of the `/etc` directory by modifying the `platform_etc_dir`.

title: Security Basics
heading: Certificate Configuration#
text: By default, Riak assumes that all certs are stored in each node’s `/etc` directory. If you are using the newer, `riak.conf`-based configuration system, you can change the location of the `/etc` directory by modifying the `platform_etc_dir`. More information can be found in our documentation on configuring directories.

title: Security Basics
heading: Certificate Configuration#
text: More information can be found in our documentation on configuring directories. Type Parameter Default Signing authority `ssl.cacertfile` `#(platform_etc_dir)/cacertfile.pem` Cert `ssl.certfile` `#(platform_etc_dir)/cert.pem` Key file `ssl.keyfile` `#(platform_etc_dir)/key.pem`

title: Security Basics
heading: Certificate Configuration#
text: If you are using the older, `app.config`-based configuration system, these paths can be set in the `ssl` subsection of the `riak_core` section. The corresponding parameters are shown in the example below: Appconfig

title: Security Basics
heading: Certificate Configuration#
text: Appconfig {riak_core, [ %% Other configs {ssl, [ {certfile, "./etc/cert.pem"}, {keyfile, "./etc/key.pem"}, {cacertfile, "./etc/cacertfile.pem"} ]}, %% Other configs ]}

title: Security Basics
heading: Referer Checks and Certificate Revocation Lists#
text: In order to provide safeguards against cross-site-scripting (XSS) and request-forgery attacks, Riak performs secure referer checks by default. Those checks make it impossible to serve data directly from Riak. To disable those checks, set the `secure_referer_check` parameter to `off`.

title: Security Basics
heading: Referer Checks and Certificate Revocation Lists#
text: Those checks make it impossible to serve data directly from Riak. To disable those checks, set the `secure_referer_check` parameter to `off`. If you are using certificate-based authentication, Riak will check the certificate revocation list (CRL) of connecting clients’ certificate by default.

title: Security Basics
heading: Referer Checks and Certificate Revocation Lists#
text: To disable those checks, set the `secure_referer_check` parameter to `off`. If you are using certificate-based authentication, Riak will check the certificate revocation list (CRL) of connecting clients’ certificate by default. To disable this behavior, set the `check_crl` parameter to `off`.

title: Managing Security Sources
text: If you’re looking for more general information on Riak Security, it may be best to start with our general guide to authentication and authorization. This document provides more granular information on the four available authentication sources in Riak Security: trusted networks, password, pluggable authentication modules (PAM), and certificates. These sources correspond to `trust`, `password`, `pam`, and `certificate`, respectively, in the `riak admin security` interface.

title: Managing Security Sources
text: This document provides more granular information on the four available authentication sources in Riak Security: trusted networks, password, pluggable authentication modules (PAM), and certificates. These sources correspond to `trust`, `password`, `pam`, and `certificate`, respectively, in the `riak admin security` interface. The examples below will assume that the network in question is `127.0.0.1/32` and that a Riak user named `riakuser` has been created and that security has been enabled.

title: Managing Security Sources
text: These sources correspond to `trust`, `password`, `pam`, and `certificate`, respectively, in the `riak admin security` interface. The examples below will assume that the network in question is `127.0.0.1/32` and that a Riak user named `riakuser` has been created and that security has been enabled. Note on SSL connections If you use any of the aforementioned security sources, even `trust`, you will need to do so via a secure SSL connection.

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Trust-based Authentication#
text: This form of authentication enables you to specify trusted CIDRs from which all clients will be authenticated by default. Bash

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Trust-based Authentication#
text: Bash riak admin security add-source all 127.0.0.1/32 trust

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Trust-based Authentication#
text: Here, we have specified that anyone connecting to Riak from the designated CIDR (in this case `localhost`) will be successfully authenticated: Curl

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Trust-based Authentication#
text: Curl curl https://localhost:8098/types/<type>/buckets/<bucket>/keys/<key>

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Trust-based Authentication#
text: If this request returns `not found` or a Riak object, then things have been set up appropriately. You can specify any number of trusted networks in the same fashion. You can also specify users as trusted users, as in the following example:

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Trust-based Authentication#
text: You can specify any number of trusted networks in the same fashion. You can also specify users as trusted users, as in the following example: Bash

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Trust-based Authentication#
text: Bash riak admin security add-source riakuser 127.0.0.1/32 trust

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Trust-based Authentication#
text: Now, `riakuser` can interact with Riak without providing credentials. Here’s an example in which only the username is passed to Riak: Curl

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Trust-based Authentication#
text: Curl curl -u riakuser: \ https://localhost:8098/types/<type>/buckets/<bucket>/keys/<key>

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Authenticating via the `password` source requires that our `riakuser` be given a password. `riakuser` can be assigned a password upon creation, as in this example: Bash

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Bash riak admin security add-user riakuser password=captheorem4life

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Or a password can be assigned to an already existing user by modifying that user’s characteristics: Bash

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Bash riak admin security alter-user riakuser password=captheorem4life

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: You can specify that all users must authenticate themselves via password when connecting to Riak from `localhost`: Bash

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Bash riak admin security add-source all 127.0.0.1/32 password

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Or you can specify that any number of specific users must do so: Bash

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Bash riak admin security add-source riakuser 127.0.0.1/32 password riak admin security add-source otheruser 127.0.0.1/32 password # etc

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Now, our `riakuser` must enter a username and password to have any access to Riak whatsoever: Curl

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Curl curl -u riakuser:captheorem4life \ https://localhost:8098/types/<type>/buckets/<bucket>/keys/<key>

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: This form of authentication (`certificate`) requires that Riak and a specified client—or clients—interacting with Riak bear certificates signed by the same Root Certificate Authority. Note At this time, client certificates are not supported in Riak’s HTTP interface, and can be used only through the protocol buffers interface.

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: Note At this time, client certificates are not supported in Riak’s HTTP interface, and can be used only through the protocol buffers interface. Let’s specify that our user `riakuser` is going to be authenticated using a certificate on `localhost`:

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: At this time, client certificates are not supported in Riak’s HTTP interface, and can be used only through the protocol buffers interface. Let’s specify that our user `riakuser` is going to be authenticated using a certificate on `localhost`: Bash

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: Bash riak admin security add-source riakuser 127.0.0.1/32 certificate

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: When the `certificate` source is used, `riakuser` must also be entered as the common name, aka `CN`, that you specified when you generated your certificate, as in the following OpenSSL example: Bash

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: Bash openssl req -new ... '/CN=riakuser'

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: You can add a `certificate` source to any number of clients, as long as their `CN` and Riak username match. On the server side, you need to configure Riak by specifying a path to your certificates. First, copy all relevant files to your Riak cluster.

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: On the server side, you need to configure Riak by specifying a path to your certificates. First, copy all relevant files to your Riak cluster. The default directory for certificates is `/etc`, though you can specify a different directory in your `riak.conf` by either uncommenting those lines if you choose to use the defaults or setting the paths yourself:

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: First, copy all relevant files to your Riak cluster. The default directory for certificates is `/etc`, though you can specify a different directory in your `riak.conf` by either uncommenting those lines if you choose to use the defaults or setting the paths yourself: Riakconf

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: Riakconf ssl.certfile = /path/to/cert.pem ssl.keyfile = /path/to/key.pem ssl.cacertfile = /path/to/cacert.pem

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: In the client-side example above, the client’s `CN` and Riak username needed to match. On the server (i.e. Riak) side, the `CN` specified on each node must match the node’s name as registered by Riak. You can find the node’s name in `riak.conf` under the parameter `nodename`.

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: On the server (i.e. Riak) side, the `CN` specified on each node must match the node’s name as registered by Riak. You can find the node’s name in `riak.conf` under the parameter `nodename`. And so if the `nodename` for a cluster is `riak-node-1`, you would need to generate your certificate with that in mind, as in this OpenSSL example:

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: You can find the node’s name in `riak.conf` under the parameter `nodename`. And so if the `nodename` for a cluster is `riak-node-1`, you would need to generate your certificate with that in mind, as in this OpenSSL example: Bash

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: Bash openssl req -new ... '/CN=riak-node-1'

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: Once certificates have been properly generated and configured on all of the nodes in your Riak cluster, you need to perform a rolling restart. Once that process is complete, you can use the client certificate that you generated for the user `riakuser`. How to use Riak clients in conjunction with OpenSSL and other certificates varies from client library to client library.

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: Once that process is complete, you can use the client certificate that you generated for the user `riakuser`. How to use Riak clients in conjunction with OpenSSL and other certificates varies from client library to client library. We strongly recommend checking the documentation of your client library for further information.

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: PAM-based Authentication#
text: This section assumes that you have set up a PAM service bearing the name `riak_pam`, e.g. by creating a `pam.d/riak_pam` service definition specifying `auth` and/or other PAM services set up to authenticate a user named `riakuser`. As in the certificate-based authentication example above, the user’s name must be the same in both your authentication module and in Riak Security. If we want the user `riakuser` to use this PAM service on `localhost`, we need to add a `pam` security source in Riak and specify the name of the service:

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: PAM-based Authentication#
text: As in the certificate-based authentication example above, the user’s name must be the same in both your authentication module and in Riak Security. If we want the user `riakuser` to use this PAM service on `localhost`, we need to add a `pam` security source in Riak and specify the name of the service: Bash

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: PAM-based Authentication#
text: Bash riak admin security add-source all 127.0.0.1/32 pam service=riak_pam

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: PAM-based Authentication#
text: Note: If you do not specify a name for your PAM service, Riak will use the default, which is `riak`. To verify that the source has been properly specified: Bash

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: PAM-based Authentication#
text: Bash riak admin security print-sources

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: PAM-based Authentication#
text: That command should output the following: Text

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: PAM-based Authentication#
text: You can test that setup most easily by using `curl`. A normal request to Riak without specifying a user will return an `Unauthorized` message: Curl

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: PAM-based Authentication#
text: Curl curl -u riakuser: \ https://localhost:8098/types/<type>/buckets/<bucket>/keys/<key>

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: PAM-based Authentication#
text: Response: Text

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: PAM-based Authentication#
text:
Text 401 Unauthorized

Unauthorized

Unauthorized

mochiweb+webmachine web server

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: PAM-based Authentication#
text: If you identify yourself as `riakuser` and are successfully authenticated by your PAM service, you should get either `not found` or a Riak object if one is stored in the specified bucket type/bucket/key path: Curl

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: PAM-based Authentication#
text: Curl curl -u riakuser:<pam_password> \ https://localhost:8098/types/<type>/buckets/<bucket>/keys/<key>

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: How Sources Are Applied#
text: When managing security sources—any of the sources explained above—you always have the option of applying a source to either a single user, multiple users, or all users (`all`). If specific users and `all` have no sources in common, this presents no difficulty. But what happens if one source is applied to `all` and a different source is applied to a specific user?

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: How Sources Are Applied#
text: If specific users and `all` have no sources in common, this presents no difficulty. But what happens if one source is applied to `all` and a different source is applied to a specific user? The short answer is that the more specifically assigned source—i.e. to the user—will be consider a user’s security source.

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: How Sources Are Applied#
text: But what happens if one source is applied to `all` and a different source is applied to a specific user? The short answer is that the more specifically assigned source—i.e. to the user—will be consider a user’s security source. We’ll illustrate that with the following example, in which the `certificate` source is assigned to `all`, but the `password` source is assigned to `riakuser`:

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: How Sources Are Applied#
text: The short answer is that the more specifically assigned source—i.e. to the user—will be consider a user’s security source. We’ll illustrate that with the following example, in which the `certificate` source is assigned to `all`, but the `password` source is assigned to `riakuser`: Bash

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: How Sources Are Applied#
text: Bash riak admin security add-source all 127.0.0.1/32 certificate riak admin security add-source riakuser 127.0.0.1/32 password

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: How Sources Are Applied#
text: If we run `riak admin security print-sources`, we’ll get the following output: Text

title: Managing Security Sources
heading: How Sources Are Applied#
text: As we can see, `password` is set as the security source for `riakuser`, whereas everyone else will authenticate using `certificate`.

title: HTTP 204
text: In the HTTP standard, a `204 No Content` is returned when the request was successful but there is nothing to return other than HTTP headers. If you add `returnbody=true` in the `PUT` request, you will receive a `200 OK` and the content you just stored, otherwise you will receive a `204 No Content`.
